The enhanced two-step floating catchment area (E2SFCA) index gives each place
the GP supply per resident within reach, with weights that fall with travel
time. This guide rebuilds the index of [Getting started](spax.html) one step
at a time from the building blocks of spax, and compares the result with
`spax()`. By the end you can say where each cell's number comes from, swap
one set of weights to get another index, and see why the calculation has to
cover the whole study area. The inputs are the mainland grids of [The Cornwall
GP example data](cornwall-data.html). The `spax()` interface and the
allocation model are experimental and may change in later versions.

```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
```

## The formula

A floating catchment area (FCA) index has two steps. First each facility
gathers the demand around it and divides its supply by that demand. Then each
place adds up the ratios of the facilities it can reach. Here demand is the
residents of a grid cell and supply is a practice's GP full-time equivalents
(FTE).

Let demand at cell $i$ be $D_i$ and supply at practice $j$ be $S_j$. The
weights $G_{ij}$ decide how much of cell $i$'s demand practice $j$ gathers,
and the weights $H_{ij}$ how much of practice $j$'s ratio cell $i$ receives.
Then

\[
L_j=\sum_i D_iG_{ij},\qquad R_j=S_j/L_j,\qquad A_i=\sum_j H_{ij}R_j.
\]

$L_j$ is the demand practice $j$ gathers, $R_j$ its supply-to-demand ratio
and $A_i$ the index at cell $i$. E2SFCA uses the same decay weights $W_{ij}$,
which fall with the travel time from cell $i$ to practice $j$ (step 1), for
both: $G = H = W$.

## The inputs

The setup code shared by every grid guide, explained in [The Cornwall GP
example data](cornwall-data.html), reads the population grid, the mainland
practices and one layer of travel minutes per practice. The supply is also
kept as a vector named by practice code, and a small helper maps a layer
around Truro so that single cells stay visible.

```{r inputs}
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel_grid <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")[[gp$practice]]
# Keep cells with a travel time to every mainland practice
pop <- trim(mask(pop, sum(travel_grid)))
travel_grid <- crop(travel_grid, pop)
grid_data <- prep_data(pop, gp, travel_grid, id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")

# GP FTE named by practice code
supply <- setNames(gp$gp_fte_extg, gp$practice)

# Map helper: a layer within the Truro display window, with practices
truro_window <- ext(-5.30, -4.80, 50.12, 50.42)
practices <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  vect()
coast <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_union() |>
  vect()
show <- function(layer, title) {
  plot(
    crop(layer, truro_window),
    axes = FALSE,
    main = title,
    col = hcl.colors(50, "viridis")
  )
  lines(crop(coast, truro_window), lwd = 0.6)
  points(crop(practices, truro_window), pch = 3, col = "red")
}
```

The calculation covers all of mainland Cornwall. Only the maps zoom in.

## Step 1: decay weights

With Gaussian decay, $W_{ij}=\exp\!\left(-d_{ij}^2/(2\sigma^2)\right)$, where
$d_{ij}$ is the
travel time and σ is the travel scale. We use σ = 10 minutes, a choice for
this guide. `calc_decay()` works on plain numbers and on rasters alike.

```{r kernel, fig.alt = "Raster map of the area around Truro showing the Gaussian decay weight of one central Truro practice, from 0 to 1: close to 1 near the practice and fading with travel time, with gaps along the estuaries; red crosses mark the practices."}
# The weight left after a few travel times
minutes <- c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30)
weight_left <- calc_decay(minutes, method = "gaussian", sigma = 10)
round(setNames(weight_left, minutes), 3)

# The same decay applied to every travel layer
weights <- calc_decay(travel_grid, method = "gaussian", sigma = 10)
show(
  weights[["L82001"]],
  "Step 1: weight of one Truro practice (L82001), 0 to 1"
)
```

A practice 10 minutes away keeps `r round(100 * weight_left[3])`% of the
weight it would have next door, and one 30 minutes away about
`r round(100 * weight_left[6])`%. Each practice has one weight layer. The map
shows the layer for L82001, a practice in central Truro: it is the red cross
at the center of the bright area (the other crosses are other practices). The
weight is close to 1 near it and fades with travel time. The shape follows the
travel-time surface rather than straight-line distance, and the gaps are
estuaries.

## Step 2 (optional): normalize the demand-side weights

The weights of all practices at one cell can add up to more than 1. Where
many practices are close, each of them counts the same resident.
`calc_normalize()` can rescale them: `"standard"` (its default) divides each
cell's weights by their sum, and `"semi"` does so only where the sum exceeds
1. `"identity"`, the default of `spec_e2sfca()`, leaves them as they are. The
table gives cell quantiles of the summed weights, before and after.

```{r normalize}
# Sum of all practices' weights at each cell
cell_sum <- function(layers) values(sum(layers), mat = FALSE)
probs <- c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)

standard <- calc_normalize(weights, method = "standard")
semi <- calc_normalize(weights, method = "semi")

round(
  rbind(
    identity = quantile(cell_sum(weights), probs, na.rm = TRUE),
    standard = quantile(cell_sum(standard), probs, na.rm = TRUE),
    semi = quantile(cell_sum(semi), probs, na.rm = TRUE)
  ),
  2
)
```

```{r normalize-values, include = FALSE}
identity_sums <- quantile(cell_sum(weights), probs, na.rm = TRUE)
```

At the median cell the weights sum to `r sprintf("%.2f", identity_sums[[2]])`, and
even at the 5th percentile they sum to `r sprintf("%.2f", identity_sums[[1]])`. So
`"standard"` and `"semi"` give almost the same result here, and both differ
from `"identity"`. The choice changes the demand each practice gathers and so
the index: normalization is part of the model you choose.
`spec_e2sfca(normalize = )` applies it to the demand side only. We keep
`"identity"`, the default, so $G = H = W$.

## Step 3: gather demand to practices

`gather_weighted()` sums demand times weight over all cells for each practice:
$L_j=\sum_i D_iW_{ij}$. With `simplify = TRUE` it returns a vector named by the
weight layers.

```{r gather}
gathered <- gather_weighted(
  values = pop,
  weights = weights,
  simplify = TRUE  # one named value per practice
)
round(head(gathered))
```

The names are the practice codes, which step 4 uses to line up the supply.
Each value is the weighted number of residents a practice gathers. A resident
within reach of several practices counts toward each of them, so these values,
over all `r length(gathered)` practices, add up to
`r round(sum(gathered) / sum(values(pop), na.rm = TRUE), 1)` times the
mainland's residents.

## Step 4: supply-to-demand ratios

Each practice's ratio is its supply over the demand it gathered, $R_j=S_j/L_j$.
Index the supply by the names of `gathered`, not by position. The table shows
six practices near Truro.

```{r ratio}
ratio <- supply[names(gathered)] / gathered

# Supply, gathered demand and ratio for six practices near Truro
near_truro <- c("L82001", "L82028", "L82015", "L82061", "L82045", "L82048")
data.frame(practice = near_truro) |>
  left_join(select(gp, practice, name), by = "practice") |>
  mutate(
    gp_fte = round(supply[practice], 1),
    weighted_residents = round(gathered[practice]),
    fte_per_1000 = round(1000 * ratio[practice], 2)
  )
```

The ratios look small because, with identity weights, each resident is
counted by several practices. Step 5 adds them back up. The two central Truro
practices share one site, so they gather the same demand. With a decay that
reaches zero, such as a fixed catchment, a practice can gather no demand.
spax gives it a ratio of zero, but the division above gives `Inf`, so set
those ratios to 0 when you calculate by hand.

## Step 5: spread the ratios back to cells

`spread_weighted()` multiplies each practice's ratio by its weight layer and
sums over practices: $A_i=\sum_j W_{ij}R_j$. It matches values to layers by
position, so pass the ratios in layer order.

```{r spread, fig.alt = "Raster map of the E2SFCA index around Truro in GP FTE per 1,000 residents, with practices as red crosses; values are highest in a band from Truro towards the south-west and lower in the east of the window."}
# Ratios in layer order, without names: matching is by position
access <- spread_weighted(
  values = unname(ratio[names(weights)]),
  weights = weights
)
show(1000 * access, "Step 5: E2SFCA, GP FTE per 1,000 residents")
```

The index is highest in a band west and south-west of Truro and falls towards
the east of the window, where fewer practices are close. A cell's index is a sum
of contributions from every practice. For the cell
that contains the central Truro practice, the largest contributions are, in GP
FTE per 1,000 residents:

```{r contributions}
# The grid cell that contains practice L82001
site <- geom(practices[practices$practice == "L82001", ])
cell <- cellFromXY(pop, site[, c("x", "y"), drop = FALSE])

# Each practice's contribution: its weight at the cell times its ratio
weights_at_cell <- unlist(extract(weights, cell))
contributions <- sort(
  1000 * weights_at_cell * ratio[names(weights_at_cell)],
  decreasing = TRUE
)

round(
  c(
    head(contributions, 5),
    all_others = sum(contributions[-(1:5)]),
    total = sum(contributions)
  ),
  3
)
```

```{r contribution-values, include = FALSE}
others_share <- round(100 * sum(contributions[-(1:5)]) / sum(contributions))
```

The two practices at the central Truro site contribute most. The other
`r length(contributions) - 5` practices beyond the top five still add
`r others_share`% of the cell's index.

## The same index from `spax()`

The surface built by hand, `access`, should match the index from `spax()`,
the one-call function `spax_e2sfca()` and the more general
`compute_access()`. `compute_access()` takes the two weight sets $G$ and $H$
of the formula as `demand_weights` and `access_weights`, so it can build any
index of this form. Each comparison below prints `TRUE` when the two surfaces
agree, cell by cell and in which cells are empty.

```{r check}
# The index from a specification
by_spec <- spax(grid_data, spec_e2sfca(decay = decay_gaussian(sigma = 10)))

# The one-call function
one_call <- spax_e2sfca(
  demand = pop,
  supply = gp,
  distance = travel_grid,
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
  id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
)

# The general function, with the decay weights on both sides
general <- compute_access(
  demand = pop,
  supply = supply,
  demand_weights = weights,
  access_weights = weights
)

# Compare a surface with the one built by hand
same_as_by_hand <- function(surface) {
  all.equal(values(surface, mat = FALSE), values(access, mat = FALSE))
}
c(
  spax = same_as_by_hand(by_spec$accessibility),
  spax_e2sfca = same_as_by_hand(one_call$accessibility),
  compute_access = same_as_by_hand(general)
)
```

`all.equal()` allows for rounding error in the last digits, and every route
agrees. Each computes the same three quantities: gathered demand, ratios and
the weighted sum of ratios.

## Change the access-side weights: M2SFCA

The modified 2SFCA (M2SFCA) keeps $W$ on the demand side but uses $W^2$ on
the access side, so $G = W$ and $H = W^2$. $W^2$ is below $W$ except at zero
travel time, and far below it for distant practices, so M2SFCA discounts
cells whose practices are far away. Swap the access-side weights for their
squares and `compute_access()` gives M2SFCA.

```{r m2sfca}
m2sfca <- spax(grid_data, spec_m2sfca(decay = decay_gaussian(sigma = 10)))

# M2SFCA from the blocks: squared weights on the access side only
m2sfca_by_blocks <- compute_access(
  demand = pop,
  supply = supply,
  demand_weights = weights,
  access_weights = weights^2
)
all.equal(
  values(m2sfca_by_blocks, mat = FALSE),
  values(m2sfca$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
)
```

The two agree: M2SFCA differs from E2SFCA only in the weights of step 5.

## Other indices from the same blocks

The three-step FCA (3SFCA) and Huff-2SFCA share each cell's demand among its
practices before the two steps. `calc_choice()` turns the decay weights into **selection
weights**: each practice's share of the cell's weights, which add up to 1 at
every cell. With an attractiveness, here GP FTE, each weight is first
multiplied by it, as in the Huff model. Both indices then use the decay weight
times the selection weight in both steps, and `compute_access()` does the
rest.

```{r selection-blocks}
# 3SFCA: each cell's weights divided by their sum
selection <- calc_choice(weights)
range(values(sum(selection), mat = FALSE), na.rm = TRUE)
sfca3_weights <- weights * selection
sfca3_by_blocks <- compute_access(pop, supply, sfca3_weights, sfca3_weights)

# Huff-2SFCA: the same, with each weight times the practice's GP FTE
huff_selection <- calc_choice(weights, attractiveness = supply)
huff_weights <- weights * huff_selection
huff_by_blocks <- compute_access(pop, supply, huff_weights, huff_weights)

# The same indices from spax()
sfca3 <- spax(grid_data, spec_3sfca(decay = decay_gaussian(sigma = 10)))
huff2sfca <- spax(grid_data, spec_huff2sfca(decay = decay_gaussian(sigma = 10)))
c(
  `3SFCA` = all.equal(
    values(sfca3_by_blocks, mat = FALSE),
    values(sfca3$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
  ),
  `Huff-2SFCA` = all.equal(
    values(huff_by_blocks, mat = FALSE),
    values(huff2sfca$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
  )
)
```

The selection weights add up to 1 at every cell, as the range shows, and both
rebuilds agree with `spax()`. The same blocks build an index of your own:
any two weight stacks on the grid of the demand can go into
`compute_access()`. [Which FCA index?](fca-methods.html)
maps these indices side by side.

## Why the calculation covers the whole mainland

Cropping the inputs to the Truro window before calculating would be quicker.
But every practice, including those outside the window, would then gather only
the demand inside it. The output gives cell quantiles of the percentage
difference between the cropped and the full calculation, for cells in the
window.

```{r crop-effect}
# Calculate on the Truro window only
truro_data <- prep_data(
  crop(pop, truro_window),
  gp,
  crop(travel_grid, truro_window),
  id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
)
cropped <- spax(truro_data, spec_e2sfca(decay = decay_gaussian(sigma = 10)))

# Compare with the full calculation over the same cells
in_window <- values(crop(by_spec$accessibility, truro_window), mat = FALSE)
relative <- values(cropped$accessibility, mat = FALSE) / in_window - 1
round(quantile(100 * relative, c(0, 0.5, 1), na.rm = TRUE), 1)
```

```{r crop-values, include = FALSE}
median_rise <- round(100 * median(relative, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
smallest_rise <- round(100 * min(relative, na.rm = TRUE), 1)
worst_ratio <- round(1 + max(relative, na.rm = TRUE))
```

Every cell's index rises: by `r smallest_rise`% at the least affected cell
and `r median_rise`% at the median. The worst cell, on the window's edge,
rises to about `r worst_ratio` times its full value. It picks up practices
outside the window, whose small remaining demand gives them very high ratios.
Calculate on the full study area and crop only for display.
